quotes.text: The appeal of Beastie Boys is that they are an honest-to-god band and that is all I want out of life.

Mike D, Ad-Rock (Adam Horovitz) and MCA (Adam Yauch) did start out in 1981 as a hardcore band, an origin story that shows up musically time to time in their later material, including this reissue of Ill Communication.

The Beasties went on to have a charmed career, helping put Def Jam Recordings, helmed by Russell Simmons and Rick Rubin, on the map and going on to release a sequence of LPs that continually superseded each other in different ways.
A maturity and purpose had taken hold, largely guided by Yauch, who was older and more of a spiritual adventurer and leader as recounted by Horovitz in Beastie Boys Book (2018).

Their 1986 debut, License to Ill, quickly established their fame with frat boy numbers like "Girls," "Brass Monkey," "No Sleep till Brooklyn" and, above all, "(You Gotta) Fight for Your Right (To Party!)." Pivotal in bringing hip hop to white audiences, the LP's appeal rested in its sampling of hard rock, specifically bands like Led Zeppelin, along with expressing a bro-ishness that was both serious and self-deprecating.

Their sophomore effort, Paul's Boutique, went in an entirely different direction with its dense sampling and layered production. Recorded in Los Angeles with the relatively unknown Dust Brothers, it has since been appraised as the Beastie Boys' masterpiece, as hip hop's answer to Sgt. Pepper's given its heavy studio pedigree.
While there is a strong case for this evaluation, Ill Communication has a looseness and tactile performativity that is absent on its esteemed predecessor.
Check Your Head, an album promoted as having MCA et al. returning to their instruments—enough with studio tricks—and Ill Communication continues this trajectory.
The exuberant single "Sabotage" captures this ethos and the energy of the album as a whole. It may well be the defining statement of the Beasties' career, among many emblematic possibilities.
"Root Down – Free Zone Mix" has a minor key vibe that is unusual in their upbeat oeuvre.
"Sure Shot – European B-Boy Mix" is similarly stripped down in a way that conveys an unexpectedly bleak quality.
As discussed in Beastie Boys Book, the song was originally intended to be instrumental with lyrics added later.
The world has changed since Manhattan's darkest day, but then so has this trio of once and future smartasses. They used to make you laugh; now they're capable of making you cry as well.
a 90 minutes-plus barrage of career-spanning East Coast brilliance

Clearly, they are attempting a transition from snotty-nosed brats to serious musicians. The Beasties began to show signs of such aspiration with their follow-up album to "Licensed to Ill," 1989's "Paul's Boutique," where they attempted to move beyond sheer humor and attitude and to explore different musical textures.
The exploration continues with the group's current release, "Check Your Head." On several cuts, the three young rappers even play musical instruments.

Monday's show turned out to be a rather awkward collage of the Beastie Boys' changing faces as they moved back and forth between their various incarnations as rappers, punk rockers and funky musicians.
Musically, the Beasties have a long way to go before they can carry a show primarily with sound.
the rap of Mike D, King Ad-Rock and MCA is deliberately crude, rude and obnoxious.
Rap is simple, it relies on attitude and it gives you the sense that anybody can do it
the Beasties have made this breakthrough without compromising or sanitizing their music

The performance itself was pretty basic, with nonstop action and aggression making up for the sameness of their sing-song rapping. With high-volume backing supplied by a deejay atop the Bud cans, and visual support from a woman dancing in a big bird cage, the Beasties hunched and stalked and slid and carried off their 40 minutes pretty well.
the Beastie Boys have yanked rebellion from its heavy-metal and punk ghettos and returned it to the mainstream.
